responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character07_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Sure. Speaking as Character07_M—

When I think about 'fairness,' it’s honestly a word that hits home, you know? For me, fairness isn’t just some abstract idea—it’s about people getting a real shot, no matter where they start from. Growing up Black and lower middle class, I’ve seen how systems aren’t always fair—whether it’s jobs, schools, or just walking down the street. So, to me, fairness means breaking down those barriers that keep folks out or push them down. It’s about holding the door open for the next person, not just making sure I get mine.

As for 'belonging,' that’s another big one. I know what it’s like to feel like you’re on the outside, to always wonder if you really fit in somewhere—because of how you look, where you’re from, or the money your family has. So when I talk about belonging, I’m talking about building spaces where people don’t have to question if they’re wanted. Where you can walk into a room and nobody’s side-eyeing you because you’re Black or you talk a certain way. A genuine sense of belonging is when you’re valued for who you are, not just tolerated.

Community, to me, is about looking out for each other. It’s about having each other’s backs—whether it’s your neighbor who lost their job, the kid who’s struggling in school, or folks who just moved in and don’t know anyone yet. My experience growing up is that we didn’t always have much, but what we did have, we shared. Community isn’t just about the people who look or live like you, either. It’s about recognizing our struggles are connected, that we rise and fall together. That’s what I try to live and what I want to see more of.

When I think back, what stands out are those moments where I saw people step up for each other, even when it wasn’t easy. Like organizing a block clean-up, or mentoring younger kids so they could dodge some of the trouble that comes with feeling left out. Or just speaking up when something’s not right, even if you catch heat for it. That’s what fairness, belonging, and community look like to me—fighting for more than just yourself, making sure everybody has a seat at the table.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character07_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Honestly, sitting out here and seeing all kinds of folks—old, young, people who grew up around here and folks who just moved in, all different backgrounds—it makes me feel a mix of hope and challenge.

I’m not gonna pretend it’s always easy. Sometimes there are moments where I feel out of place, or like people don’t quite get where I’m coming from. But mostly, I see it as a good thing. Diversity in the neighborhood means there’s a lot to learn from each other. I grew up used to people who looked like me and shared my experiences, but over time I’ve come to appreciate hearing different stories, different perspectives. It keeps things real and reminds me that everybody’s got their own struggles and dreams.

I like when people are open and willing to connect—even if it’s just a “how you doing?” or sharing some food at a cookout. That’s how barriers come down. Sure, there are moments of awkwardness, sometimes even tension—especially if folks hold on to stereotypes or don’t try to understand each other. But if we show up with respect and a little patience, those walls get chipped away.

Bottom line is, I feel good about living in a place where people are different. It’s not about pretending we’re all the same, but about being willing to listen and stick together when it counts. That’s what makes a neighborhood strong, in my eyes. And I want to be someone who adds to that, not someone who puts up more walls.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah, I’m willing to talk about that.

Honestly, when you’ve got all kinds of people living side by side—folks dealing with tough stuff like addiction, health problems, or just living a way that’s different from what you’re used to—it can be a lot. But I don’t think the answer is to judge or avoid people. I’ve seen firsthand that you never know what someone’s carrying until you hear their story.

What makes everyone comfortable, in my view, is keeping things real but respectful. You greet folks, show some kindness, and don’t make a big deal out of their situation or background. If someone’s struggling—say, with alcoholism or something similar—you try not to turn away or treat them like they’re less than human. You don’t have to agree with everyone’s choices, but you meet them where they are. Same goes for people with infectious diseases or folks with different sexual orientations or living situations. Respect goes a long way.

There are definitely times when more communication and tolerance are needed. Like, if neighbors start talking behind someone’s back, or refusing to interact because of prejudice or fear, that’s when things get ugly. I think it helps to talk things through—sometimes at a community meeting, sometimes just one-on-one. If there’s tension, put it on the table, don’t let it fester. And for stuff people don’t understand—like a different religion or language, or why someone lives the way they do—it’s better to ask questions respectfully than make assumptions.

The reason I feel this way is because, growing up, I saw what happens when folks get pushed out or judged for stuff they can’t control. It doesn’t help anybody. We all got struggles, some just show up in different ways. So if we want a real sense of community, we have to be willing to give each other a little grace and be open to learning. That’s not always easy, but it’s necessary if we want a neighborhood that feels like home for everyone.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character07_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a tough question, and it’s something I think about a lot.

When jobs are tight and folks are worried about putting food on the table, fairness starts feeling personal. For me, fairness means making sure the people who’ve been here, who’ve built up the community and paid their dues, aren’t pushed to the side. Local residents—folks who’ve worked hard, maybe struggling for years—shouldn’t just be forgotten when things get tough.

But I also know migrant workers are out here trying to survive and support their families, just like anybody else. And a lot of times, they’re doing jobs others might not want, or they’re bringing skills that help the community move forward. So I don’t see it as locals vs. migrants in some cutthroat way.

If I was in charge, I’d look for a balance where jobs are fairly open, but certain protections exist for local workers—like job training, fair wages, and making sure companies aren’t exploiting anybody just to save a buck. Maybe there’s a way to prioritize residents for some openings, but also have clear, fair pathways for migrants to work legally and contribute. I’d want policies that stop employers from pitting people against each other, driving down wages, or ignoring safety and rights.

End of the day, fairness means not blaming migrants for problems caused by bigger issues—like corporations cutting corners or governments not investing in communities. We have to spread resources smartly and make sure no one’s left behind, but also recognize everyone’s humanity. It’s not easy, but with honest policies and open dialogue, I think we can find a way that respects both locals and migrants.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character07_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Alright, looking at it from a bigger picture—as Character07_M, I get why people feel so many different ways about immigration. It’s complicated.

First off, I think it’s true that immigrants fill a lot of jobs that keep this country running. You see it in food service, construction, healthcare—jobs that a lot of folks overlook but that really matter. That’s a reasonable point, and I respect it. Same goes for the argument about cultural diversity—it makes places more interesting, brings new ideas, new food, new ways of thinking. That’s a plus in my book.

On the humanitarian side, I feel strongly about helping people escaping violence, poverty, or political mess. If you’ve ever struggled or seen your own folks struggle, it’s hard not to feel for refugees or people just trying to survive. So I’m all for policies that give people a chance if they truly need help.

Now, on the concerns about security—crime rates, social tensions, terrorism—I think those get thrown around a lot, sometimes with facts, sometimes just out of fear. I’m not saying those concerns should be ignored, but I don’t buy into the idea that immigrants automatically bring more crime or are some kind of threat. Most people coming here just want a better life. I think that viewpoint needs real evidence, not just rumors or stereotypes. If there are issues, we should look at the real numbers and talk about solutions that focus on everybody’s safety, not just shutting people out.

About jobs and income—yeah, people worry that too much immigration could make it harder for locals to find work or drive wages down, especially for folks already struggling. That’s a real concern. But from what I’ve seen and read, it’s not always so simple; sometimes immigrants help the economy grow, sometimes there’s competition. More research and honesty are needed here.

Overall, I think the reasonable viewpoints are the ones that look at both the benefits and challenges with facts and compassion. The ones that get me worried are those based mostly on fear or stereotypes. Those need more dialogue, more evidence, and maybe just more people getting to know each other. It’s easy to blame what you don’t understand, so I’d push for conversations and education, not just jumping to conclusions.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character07_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If I had to choose, I wouldn’t go for complete openness, and I definitely wouldn’t support just flat-out refusing workers from other countries. That doesn’t sit right with me—feels like shutting the door on people who might need help or have something to offer.

What makes most sense to me is a mix: admitting people based on job demand but with some reasonable limits in place. We should look at what the country actually needs—where there are real gaps in the workforce, where industries can’t find enough local workers, and let immigrants fill those spots. But we’d need to keep an eye on things so it's not just employers taking advantage and driving down wages for everyone, locals and immigrants alike.

Setting numerical limits makes sense too, so we don’t put too much stress on schools, housing, and other resources. It’s not about keeping people out for the sake of it, but making sure folks who come here can actually integrate and build a life, and so local communities don’t feel overwhelmed or ignored.

I'd also want policies that help immigrants adjust—language classes, support for finding housing, protections against discrimination. Social integration matters, and if we just let people in without helping them find their place, that’s asking for tension.

So, my ideal policy would mix job-based entry with some limits, but always leave room for refugees and folks who need real help. Fairness is making opportunities available, but also making sure nobody gets left behind—either the people who grew up here or those just arriving. It’s about balance, watching out for each other, and making sure the system works for real people, not just the powerful or the lucky.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character07_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character07_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Honestly, stepping into Character07_M’s shoes like this made me think more deeply about how personal experiences shape the way we see things like fairness and immigration. Speaking as him, I was reminded how much a sense of being on the margins—growing up Black, lower middle class—really affects how you judge questions of belonging and opportunity. It’s not just about policy or numbers; it’s about the day-to-day feeling of being seen, or not, and what it means to share space with people different from you.

What stood out was how Character07_M would always come back to balance—being protective of his own community but also empathetic to others. He wanted policies that considered the realities of local life, but he was also insistent on not shutting the door on people who were struggling, because he understood what that felt like. Playing his role made me appreciate the need to hold space for different truths at once, instead of just picking a side.

It’s also made me reflect on my own views. I realize I sometimes focus more on the big-picture policies and less on what it feels like for people actually living in these situations. Character07_M’s way of thinking—grounded in lived experience, aware of the struggles but not losing his humanity—reminds me that good policy has to keep real people at the center.

So I guess I gained a stronger sense of how empathy and fairness can coexist, and how important it is to keep talking, listening, and not just settling for easy answers. That’s something I want to take forward, both in how I remember him and in how I approach these issues myself.
